q: This theorem is proved by induction using the fact that a sum of two binomial coefficients equals a coefficient in the next row of a triangle. It gives the coefficient of x to the k in the expansion of the sum of x and y raised to the n as n choose k. For n equal to 4, the coefficients are 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. For 10 points, name this theorem about expanding powers of a sum of two terms.

The sum of these quantities for a polygon with n sides is 180 times n minus 2 degrees. This is why the three of them in a triangle sum to 180 degrees. A hexagon has six of them summing to 720 degrees. For 10 points, name these angles found inside a closed figure at the vertices.

This number, equal to 2 times 3 times 5 times 7, is the product of the first four primes. It is the smallest number divisible by each of 2, 3, 5, and 7. Half of it is 105. For 10 points, name this number, the product of the first four primes.

This mathematician proved that the number of primes is infinite in his Elements, and also gave an algorithm for the greatest common divisor of two numbers. He is called the father of geometry. For 10 points, name this Greek mathematician who wrote the Elements.

Conic sections include the parabola, the hyperbola, and this curve. It is defined as the set of points for which the sum of distances to two fixed foci is constant. A circle is a special case with both foci at the same point. For 10 points, name this oval-shaped conic section, the shape of planetary orbits.

This theorem states that in a right triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. A 3-4-5 triangle is a common example. For 10 points, name this theorem named for a Greek philosopher from Samos.

A function f is called one of these if f of negative x equals negative f of x, so its graph is symmetric about the origin. The sine function and x cubed are examples, while cosine is not. The product of two such functions is even. For 10 points, name this type of function, the counterpart to an even function.

This sequence begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. The ratios of consecutive terms approach the golden ratio. Each term is the sum of the two before it. For 10 points, name this sequence introduced to Europe in the Liber Abaci by a mathematician from Pisa.

In a set of numbers, this measure of center is found by listing the values in order and taking the one in the middle. For 1, 3, 5, 7, 100 it equals 5, unaffected by the outlier. For 10 points, name this statistic distinct from the mean and the mode.

This number, approximately 3.14159, is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. It is irrational and transcendental. It is celebrated on March 14. For 10 points, name this constant represented by a Greek letter.

This mathematician posed a "last theorem" in a margin of a copy of Arithmetica, claiming that no three positive integers satisfy a to the n plus b to the n equals c to the n for n greater than 2. A proof was finally given by Andrew Wiles. For 10 points, name this French lawyer and mathematician.

This function is defined for positive integers as the product of all positive integers up to n, and Euler extended it to the complex numbers with an integral. Zero of these is defined as 1. Five of these is 120. For 10 points, name this function written with an exclamation point.

The Pythagorean identity states that sine squared plus this function squared equals 1. It is the ratio of adjacent side to hypotenuse in a right triangle. Its graph is a sine wave shifted by a quarter period. For 10 points, name this trigonometric function abbreviated cos.
A polygon with five sides is called this. A famous United States military headquarters has this shape. Its interior angles each measure 108 degrees if it is regular. For 10 points, name this shape.

This operation on a function gives the slope of the tangent line at each point. For x squared, the result is 2x. It was developed independently by Newton and Leibniz. For 10 points, name this basic operation of calculus, whose reverse is integration.

The set of numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and 13 are examples of these numbers, which have exactly two positive divisors. Two is the only even one. For 10 points, name this type of number that is only divisible by one and itself.

These numbers are written as a plus b i, where i is the square root of negative one. They can be plotted on the Argand plane. The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra says polynomials factor completely over this set. For 10 points, name this extension of the real numbers.

Cardano published a formula for the roots of this kind of polynomial equation, which Tartaglia had shown him. The general form has a term in x cubed and its graph can have up to two turning points. Abel and Galois later showed no such formula exists for degree five. For 10 points, name this degree-three kind of equation.

The area of a circle with radius 5 is 25 pi. The distance across a circle through its center is called this. It equals twice the radius. For 10 points, name this length, a chord passing through the center.

The probability of two independent events both occurring is found by doing this operation to their separate probabilities. For example, getting two heads in a row on fair coin flips has probability one fourth. For 10 points, name this operation, repeated addition.

This mathematician is the namesake of a point set that is the intersection of the original unit interval after repeatedly removing middle thirds. He also introduced the theory that some infinities are larger than others, proving the reals are uncountable. For 10 points, name this German founder of set theory.

The set of numbers 1, 2, 3, and so on that we use to count are called these numbers. Together with zero they are the whole numbers. For 10 points, name these numbers, which contrast with the integers that include negatives.

A square matrix has this quantity, which for the two by two matrix with entries a, b, c, d equals a d minus b c. If it equals zero, the matrix has no inverse. For 10 points, name this scalar value of a matrix.

In probability, this theorem says that the probability of A given B equals the probability of B given A times the probability of A, all divided by the probability of B. It is used to update beliefs given evidence. For 10 points, name this theorem named for an English reverend.

The number of degrees in a full turn around a circle is this number. It is also the number of days approximately in a year in the old Babylonian calendar. For 10 points, name this number, equal to 6 times 60.

This type of sequence has a constant ratio between consecutive terms, such as 2, 6, 18, 54. The sum of infinitely many terms converges if the absolute value of the ratio is less than one. For 10 points, name this kind of sequence, distinct from an arithmetic one.

John Napier introduced this function to simplify multiplication into addition, and slide rules rely on it. It is the inverse of an exponential, so the base ten version of it applied to 1000 equals 3. The natural version uses the number e as its base. For 10 points, name this function written log.

This number is the smallest positive integer, and it is neither prime nor composite. It is the multiplicative identity, so multiplying any number by it leaves that number unchanged. Its reciprocal is itself. For 10 points, name this number, which comes after zero and before two.

This mathematician's namesake paradox concerns the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. He co-wrote Principia Mathematica with Alfred North Whitehead. For 10 points, name this British logician and philosopher.

In geometry, two triangles are called this if their corresponding angles are equal and their sides are in proportion, such as a triangle and an enlarged copy of it. Congruent triangles are a special case. For 10 points, name this term for triangles with the same shape.

q: This data structure is accessed in last-in, first-out order, and a call of this type is how recursion stores return addresses. Its two main operations are push and pop. Running out of room in one gives a famous overflow error. For 10 points, name this data structure that also shares its name with a pile of plates.

This algorithm repeatedly steps through a list, comparing adjacent items and swapping them if out of order. Larger values "bubble" to the end on each pass. It takes quadratic time in the worst case. For 10 points, name this simple sorting algorithm with a bath-time name.

This type of loop in programming repeats a block as long as a condition remains true. Unlike a for loop, it does not necessarily have a counter. An infinite one occurs when the condition never becomes false. For 10 points, name this loop that begins with a keyword meaning "during."

This British mathematician described an abstract machine with an infinite tape and a read-write head, and also worked at Bletchley Park breaking Enigma. A test named for him asks whether a machine can imitate a human in conversation. For 10 points, name this founder of theoretical computer science.

This program translates source code written in a high-level language into machine code before the program runs. GCC is a well-known example for C. Interpreters differ in that they execute code line by line. For 10 points, name this kind of program.

Brendan Eich created this language in ten days in 1995 for Netscape. It runs in web browsers and lets pages respond to clicks, and despite a similar name it is unrelated to a coffee-named language from Sun. Node.js lets it run on servers. For 10 points, name this language.

This search algorithm repeatedly halves the interval of a sorted array by comparing the target with the middle element. It runs in logarithmic time. It fails if the array is not sorted. For 10 points, name this search algorithm that is far faster than a linear scan for sorted data.

This computer component, often called the "brain" of a computer, executes instructions. Intel and AMD make most of the ones in desktop computers. Its abbreviation stands for "central processing unit." For 10 points, name this component, abbreviated CPU.

Tim Berners-Lee invented this system in 1989 while at CERN, combining hypertext, URLs, and HTTP. Browsers like Firefox and Chrome access it. It is often confused with the Internet itself. For 10 points, name this system of linked pages, abbreviated WWW.

This type of error occurs when a program runs but does not do what the programmer intended, such as an off-by-one mistake. The term supposedly comes from a moth found in the Harvard Mark II. For 10 points, name this kind of flaw, whose removal is debugging.

A variable that can hold only true or false is called this type, named for an English mathematician who developed algebraic logic. The operations AND, OR, and NOT act on these values. For 10 points, name this data type.

This sorting algorithm picks an element called the pivot and partitions the array into smaller and larger elements, then recurses. Its average time is n log n but its worst case is quadratic. Tony Hoare invented it. For 10 points, name this sorting algorithm sometimes called partition-exchange sort.

This protocol suite underlies the Internet, with one part breaking data into packets and another handling addressing. The second part's addresses come in versions four and six. For 10 points, name this suite, abbreviated by two sets of letters separated by a slash.

This kind of memory is volatile, losing its contents when power is turned off, and is used for programs that are currently running. A typical laptop has several gigabytes of it. For 10 points, name this memory, abbreviated RAM.

Ada Lovelace wrote what is often called the first computer program for this mechanical computer designed by Charles Babbage. It was never completed in his lifetime and was to use punched cards. For 10 points, name this proposed general-purpose machine, which had an "Analytical" name.

This protocol, abbreviated HTTP, is used for web browsing, with a secure version ending in S. Pages at addresses beginning with it are fetched by browsers. For 10 points, give the full name of this protocol, whose first word is for text that links.

In a computer, a process waiting for a resource held by another process that is waiting for its resource is in this state. The classic illustration is five philosophers with forks. For 10 points, name this standstill in concurrent computing.

This data structure holds a first-in, first-out sequence, like a line at a store. Its main operations are enqueue and dequeue. Breadth-first search uses one. For 10 points, name this data structure that shares its name with a waiting line.

This kind of software, such as Windows, macOS, or Linux, manages hardware and provides services for other programs. Android and iOS are mobile examples. For 10 points, name this basic software layer, abbreviated OS.

Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie created this operating system at Bell Labs in 1969. Its philosophy includes small tools connected by pipes and everything being a file. macOS and Linux are descended from or modeled on it. For 10 points, name this operating system.

This structure consists of nodes connected by edges and has no cycles, with one special node at the top. Binary examples have at most two children per node. Heaps and file systems are organized as these. For 10 points, name this hierarchical data structure that has a root and leaves.

This programming language, created by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs, was used to rewrite an early operating system there. Its object-oriented extension by Bjarne Stroustrup has plus signs in its name. For 10 points, name this one-letter language.

A set of step-by-step instructions to solve a problem or perform a computation is called this. The word comes from the name of a Persian mathematician, al-Khwarizmi. For 10 points, give this term used for sorting and searching procedures.
This type of attack tries every possible password or key until the correct one is found. Longer passwords make it exponentially harder. For 10 points, name this attack named for its lack of subtlety.

This design principle in programming involves hiding internal details of an object and exposing only a controlled interface. It is one of the pillars of object-oriented programming, along with inheritance and polymorphism. For 10 points, name this principle that bundles data and methods together.

This language, whose name contains a hot drink, was released by Sun Microsystems and is known for "write once, run anywhere." It is distinct from JavaScript. For 10 points, name this object-oriented language.

This function in programming calls itself with a smaller input until it reaches a base case. A classic example computes factorial this way. Fibonacci can also be computed this way, though inefficiently. For 10 points, name this technique, or the type of function using it.

A hash of a password is usually stored rather than the password itself because this property of the function makes it infeasible to recover the input. Algorithms like SHA-256 are examples. For 10 points, name this type of function mapping data of arbitrary size to a fixed-size value.

A computer virus differs from this self-replicating malware, which spreads across networks without attaching to a host file. The Morris one was one of the first on the Internet. For 10 points, name this malware named for a crawling creature.

This US Navy rear admiral led the team that developed the first compiler and contributed to COBOL, a language for business. She worked on the Harvard Mark I and UNIVAC. A Navy destroyer was named for her. For 10 points, name this computer scientist known as "Amazing Grace."

q: This scientist's three laws describe motion, and he also formulated universal gravitation. His book Principia was published in 1687. A unit of force is named for him. For 10 points, name this English physicist who supposedly was inspired by a falling apple.

This property of a material describes how much mass it has per unit volume. It is measured in grams per cubic centimeter, and water has a value of one. An object floats if it has less of this than the fluid it is in. For 10 points, name this quantity found by dividing mass by volume.

This is the SI unit of force, equal to a kilogram meter per second squared. It is named for a physicist who wrote a famous book called the Principia and formulated three laws of motion. A medium apple weighs roughly one of these. For 10 points, name this unit, abbreviated N.

The scientific method begins with a testable guess called this, which an experiment then supports or refutes. It is a proposed explanation for an observation. For 10 points, name this term, often described as an "educated guess."
This scientist developed the theory of evolution by natural selection after traveling on the HMS Beagle. He wrote On the Origin of Species in 1859. For 10 points, name this English naturalist.

This French chemist and biologist developed pasteurization and a vaccine for rabies. His swan-neck flask experiments disproved spontaneous generation. For 10 points, name this scientist who is a founder of germ theory.

Zero on this SI base temperature scale is absolute zero, and water freezes at 273.15 on it. It is named for a Scottish-Irish physicist, William Thomson, who became a baron and worked on thermodynamics. For 10 points, name this unit, abbreviated K.

These instruments, invented in the Netherlands around 1608 and improved by Galileo, make distant objects appear closer. Hubble is a famous orbiting one. For 10 points, name this instrument used by astronomers.

This type of variable in an experiment is the one that the experimenter deliberately changes to see its effect. The measured outcome is the dependent one. For 10 points, name this variable, whose name begins with a word meaning "free from control."

This English chemist at King's College London produced Photograph 51, an X-ray diffraction image of DNA. Her data were used by Watson and Crick, who later won a Nobel Prize. She also studied coal and the tobacco mosaic virus. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This prefix indicates a factor of one thousand in the metric system. It is used in the unit of distance often used for road trips outside the United States, and in the unit of mass equal to about 2.2 pounds. For 10 points, name this prefix abbreviated k.

This quantity, measured in grams or kilograms, describes how much matter is in an object. It stays the same on the Moon, whereas the related quantity weight changes with gravity. It is measured with a balance. For 10 points, name this quantity, symbol m.

This Austrian monk grew thousands of pea plants in a monastery garden in Brno. He observed that traits like seed shape appear in predictable ratios, such as three to one, in the second generation. He discovered dominant and recessive traits. For 10 points, name this father of genetics.

This German physicist developed the theories of special and general relativity and the photoelectric effect explanation. He won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics. For 10 points, name this scientist famous for E equals m c squared.

This device measures temperature and is found in many medicine cabinets. Common ones use a thin column of mercury or colored alcohol in a glass tube that rises as it gets warmer. A person with a fever has a reading above about 38 degrees Celsius. For 10 points, name this instrument.

This field studies rocks, minerals, fossils, and the structure of the Earth. Charles Lyell wrote the Principles of this science and argued for gradual change over long times, an idea called uniformitarianism. James Hutton is called its father. For 10 points, name this Earth science.

This term describes a substance made of only one type of atom, such as gold or oxygen. There are 118 known types listed on the periodic table. For 10 points, name this basic substance, which cannot be broken down chemically.

This unit of energy is named for an English brewer and physicist who measured the mechanical equivalent of heat. One of these equals a newton meter, and a watt is one of them per second. For 10 points, name this SI unit of energy.
This Greek scientist, from Syracuse, is credited with a principle about buoyancy and with the cry "Eureka." He also described the lever. For 10 points, name this ancient scientist.

This process takes place in chloroplasts using the green pigment chlorophyll. Plants convert sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water into glucose and release oxygen as a byproduct. The Calvin cycle is part of it. For 10 points, name this process by which plants make their own food.
This law states that for a given amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume. It is named for an Anglo-Irish chemist. For 10 points, name this gas law.

This scale, from 0 to 14, measures how acidic or basic a solution is. Lemon juice is low on it, pure water is at seven, and bleach is high. Litmus paper and universal indicator give a rough reading. For 10 points, name this scale, whose abbreviation has a lowercase p.

This Italian scientist used a telescope to discover four moons of Jupiter, the phases of Venus, and mountains on the Moon. He supported the Copernican model and wrote the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems. He was tried by the Inquisition. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This Russian chemist created a periodic table in 1869 that arranged elements by atomic weight and left gaps for undiscovered elements. He predicted the properties of eka-aluminium, later found as gallium. Element 101 is named for him. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This is the layer of gases surrounding Earth, held in place by gravity. It is composed of about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen. Its lowest layer, the troposphere, is where weather occurs, and above it lies the stratosphere. For 10 points, name this layer.

This scientist, the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, shared the 1903 physics prize with her husband and Henri Becquerel. For 10 points, give the term for the emission of particles by unstable nuclei that they studied.
This type of energy is stored in an object because of its position, such as a book on a high shelf. It converts to kinetic energy when the object falls. For 10 points, name this energy.

This unit, equal to about 3.26 light-years, is used by astronomers for distances to stars. It is the distance at which a star shows a parallax angle of one arcsecond. Its name combines two words, parallax and second. For 10 points, name this unit.

This scientist's namesake principle states that it is impossible to know both the position and momentum of a particle exactly. He was a German physicist who helped develop quantum mechanics. For 10 points, name him.

This is the study of weather, which includes forecasting by tracking pressure systems and fronts. Practitioners use satellites, radar, and balloons to measure the atmosphere. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with meteors. For 10 points, name this atmospheric science.

q: Bluma Zeigarnik noticed that waiters remembered unpaid orders better than completed ones. That finding led to a namesake effect stating that people remember interrupted or incomplete tasks better than finished ones. Kurt Lewin was her advisor in Berlin. For 10 points, name this effect named for a Lithuanian-born psychologist.

This thinker's study of suicide divided it into egoistic, altruistic, anomic and fatalistic types. He called society a reality distinct from individuals, made of "social facts." His books include The Division of Labor in Society and The Elementary Forms of Religious Life. For 10 points, name this French founder of functionalist sociology.

This German sociologist wrote The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism. He described the "iron cage" of rationalization and defined the state as holding a monopoly on legitimate violence. For 10 points, name this author of Economy and Society.

This French thinker coined the word "sociology" and proposed the law of three stages: theological, metaphysical and positive. He founded positivism, which holds that society can be studied scientifically. For 10 points, name this man called the father of sociology.

This word, from a Greek root meaning "lawlessness," was used by Durkheim for a condition of normlessness in which social rules break down. Robert Merton later borrowed it for his strain theory of deviance. For 10 points, name this state of social instability, often seen in rapid economic upheaval.

This theory, developed from the ideas of George Herbert Mead and Herbert Blumer, holds that people create meaning through everyday face-to-face interactions using symbols such as language. For 10 points, name this micro-level perspective in sociology.

This American sociologist's book The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life compared social interaction to theater, with a "front stage" and "back stage." He also wrote Asylums and Stigma. For 10 points, name this scholar who developed the dramaturgical approach.

Charles Horton Cooley proposed this concept in which a person's self-image develops from imagining how others see and judge them. The term uses a piece of furniture found in a bathroom. For 10 points, name this "glass" concept of self.

In this kind of institution, like prisons, boot camps and mental hospitals, inmates are cut off from society and live under formal rules. Erving Goffman gave this name to such places. For 10 points, what term describes an institution that controls all aspects of its residents' lives?

Robert Merton distinguished two kinds of function: manifest functions, which are intended and recognized, and these, which are unintended and unrecognized. A university's role as a place to meet marriage partners is an example. For 10 points, name this counterpart to manifest functions.

This German thinker co-wrote The Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels. His conflict theory describes class struggle between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat. For 10 points, name this author of Das Kapital.

Marx used this term for the process by which workers in capitalism become estranged from the products of their labor, from the labor process, from other people and from themselves. For 10 points, name this concept, a word also used for feeling distant or cut off.

This sociologist wrote The Philadelphia Negro, an empirical study of a city's Black community. He coined the term "double consciousness" in The Souls of Black Folk and co-founded the NAACP. For 10 points, name this scholar who also edited the journal The Crisis.

Howard Becker popularized this theory of deviance, which says that deviance is not an act itself but a label applied by society to a person. Edwin Lemert distinguished primary from secondary deviance within it. For 10 points, name this theory, which says that being tagged an outsider can fuel further deviance.

Thorstein Veblen coined this phrase in The Theory of the Leisure Class for lavish spending on goods to display social status, such as luxury cars or designer watches. For 10 points, name this two-word term for showy buying.

Ferdinand Tonnies contrasted Gemeinschaft with this term for impersonal, contract-based society typical of big cities. The first term means "community." For 10 points, name this German term meaning "society."

This term refers to the ranking of people in a hierarchy based on wealth, power, and prestige. Caste and class systems are two examples. For 10 points, name this term, taken from the layers of rock in geology.

In a caste system, social position is determined this way, which means a person is born into a status and cannot change it through effort. For 10 points, what term, also used for status inherited from parents, describes such a "ascribed" system?

Pierre Bourdieu used this term for non-financial assets like education, taste and manners that help people gain status. He paired it with habitus in studying class reproduction. For 10 points, name this form of "capital," which includes knowing which fork to use at a formal dinner.

Robert Putnam's book Bowling Alone argued that this resource, consisting of networks, trust and civic participation, had declined in the United States. For 10 points, name this kind of "capital" provided by relationships among people.

This author argued in The Sociological Imagination that personal troubles must be linked to public issues and historical context. He also wrote The Power Elite. For 10 points, name this American sociologist, first name C. Wright.

This American social reformer co-founded Hull House in Chicago, a settlement house that aided immigrants. She shared the 1931 Nobel Peace Prize. For 10 points, name this woman, a pioneer of social work.

William Graham Sumner coined this word for the belief that one's own culture is superior and the standard for judging others. For 10 points, name this attitude, which differs from cultural relativism.

Sumner also distinguished two kinds of norms: these everyday customs, such as table manners, are not strictly enforced, while the second type has strong moral weight. For 10 points, name these casual customs, a counterpart to mores.

This sociologist's thesis, which holds that "if men define situations as real, they are real in their consequences," is named for him and his wife Dorothy. He co-wrote The Polish Peasant in Europe and America. For 10 points, name this Chicago sociologist, first name William I.

George Ritzer applied Weber's idea of rationalization to the fast food industry and coined this term built on the name of a restaurant chain. It stresses efficiency, calculability, predictability and control. For 10 points, name this "process" named for the golden arches.

Edwin Sutherland proposed this theory, which says that people learn criminal behavior from others in intimate groups, along with attitudes favorable to breaking the law. For 10 points, name this theory about learning crime, whose name contrasts with isolation.

This sociologist, a leader of the Chicago School, studied human ecology and the "marginal man." His collaborator Ernest Burgess proposed the concentric zone model of the city. For 10 points, name this man, first name Robert E.
Answer these questions about classical sociological theorists.
parts: Which French thinker wrote Suicide and The Division of Labor in Society?
Which German wrote The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism?
Which German sociologist wrote the essay The Stranger and the book The Philosophy of Money?

q: Answer these questions about sociological concepts of the self.
parts: What term names the part of sociology that studies face-to-face interaction using symbols?
Which scholar proposed the looking-glass self?
Which philosopher of Mind, Self, and Society distinguished the "I" from the "me"?

q: Answer these questions about breaking social norms.
parts: What word names behavior that violates the norms of a society?
Which sociologist proposed strain theory in his essay Social Structure and Anomie?
Which scholar wrote Outsiders and popularized labeling theory?

q: Answer these questions about social inequality.
parts: What word names a rigid, inherited system of status, as in traditional India?
Which kind of mobility describes a move up or down within the same generation's careers or class?
Which sociologist coined "cultural capital"?

q: Answer these questions about early American urban sociology.
parts: In which Illinois city was this early American school of sociology based?
Which settlement house in that city was founded by Jane Addams?
Which model of the city by Ernest Burgess divides it into rings around a central business district?

q: Answer these questions about norms and culture.
parts: What belief that one's own culture is superior is called by this term?
What term names casually enforced customs, such as manners, in Sumner's classification?
What term names norms with strong moral significance, whose violation brings serious punishment?

q: Answer these questions about Karl Marx.
parts: Which two economic classes did Marx say were in conflict under capitalism? Give either one.
What term names the Marxian concept of workers' estrangement from their labor?
What term did Marx use for the ownership of factories and tools?

q: Answer these questions about founders of sociology.
parts: Who coined the word "sociology"?
Which American scholar wrote Middletown with his wife Helen, a study of Muncie, Indiana?
Which sociologist wrote The Souls of Black Folk and coined "double consciousness"?

q: Max Weber, Karl Marx and Emile Durkheim are often called the three founders of this field. It studies human society, social relationships and institutions. For 10 points, name this social science, a word coined by Auguste Comte.

This term refers to the process by which people learn the norms, values and behaviors of their society, through family, schools and peers. For 10 points, name this lifelong process of social learning.

In this research method, a sociologist studies a group by living among its members and taking part in their activities. It is also widely used by anthropologists. For 10 points, name this method of fieldwork, called participant observation.

These groups, such as family and close friends, involve intimate, face-to-face relationships and strong emotional ties. Charles Horton Cooley named them. For 10 points, what term describes these small, intimate groups that contrast with secondary groups?

Georg Simmel wrote an essay about this figure, someone who arrives today and stays tomorrow, combining nearness and remoteness. He also wrote about the metropolis and mental life. For 10 points, name this outsider type who is both in and out of a group.

This author's Street Corner Society was a participant-observation study of Italian-American men in Boston's North End. He spent years living in the neighborhood he described. For 10 points, name this sociologist, first name William Foote.

This French thinker's book The Spirit of the Laws argued that government power should be divided among legislative, executive and judicial branches. His ideas deeply influenced the framers of the United States Constitution. For 10 points, name this Enlightenment baron, a champion of the separation of powers.

This English philosopher's Two Treatises of Government argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that people may overthrow a government that violates them. Thomas Jefferson drew on his ideas. For 10 points, name this author.

This philosopher's Leviathan described a "state of nature" in which life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." He argued people should submit to an absolute sovereign for safety. For 10 points, name this English political theorist.

This Italian Renaissance diplomat wrote a handbook for rulers arguing that it is safer for a ruler to be feared than loved. It is dedicated to Lorenzo de Medici. For 10 points, name this author of The Prince.

This practice involves drawing electoral district boundaries to favor one party or group. It is named for a Massachusetts governor and a salamander-shaped district. For 10 points, name this manipulation of districts.

In the United States, this body, created in Article II of the Constitution, has 538 members, and a candidate needs 270 of its votes to win the presidency. For 10 points, name this system in which states choose the president through electors.

Maurice Duverger observed that this kind of electoral system, where the candidate with the most votes in a district wins, tends to produce a two-party system. It is also called first-past-the-post. For 10 points, name this voting rule that elects whoever gets the most votes, even without a majority.

Under this type of electoral system, used in Israel and many European countries, parties win legislative seats in proportion to the share of votes they receive. For 10 points, name this system, abbreviated PR, that encourages multiparty politics.

In this form of government, the executive branch is chosen from and accountable to the legislature, as in the United Kingdom and Canada. The head of government is a prime minister. For 10 points, name this system that contrasts with a presidential system.

In the United States Senate, this tactic allows a senator to delay a vote through extended speech. It can be ended through a vote called cloture, which currently requires three fifths of the Senate. For 10 points, name this delaying tactic.

In this 1803 Supreme Court case, Chief Justice John Marshall established the principle of judicial review. It involved William Marbury, who did not receive his commission as justice of the peace. For 10 points, name this case also named for the Secretary of State.

This German-born scholar, author of The Origins of Totalitarianism, also coined the phrase "the banality of evil" while covering Adolf Eichmann's trial. For 10 points, name this political theorist, first name Hannah.

This term for supreme authority within a territory was formalized in the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. Jean Bodin and Hobbes helped develop it. For 10 points, name this concept, the right of a state to govern itself without outside interference.

This 1949 alliance among Western powers, including the United States, Canada and several European countries, is based on a principle that an attack on one is an attack on all. For 10 points, name this military alliance headquartered in Brussels.

This international body has five permanent members with veto power: the United States, United Kingdom, France, Russia and China. For 10 points, name this United Nations body charged with keeping international peace.

Joseph Nye coined this term for the ability to shape what others want through culture, values and diplomacy rather than force or payment. It contrasts with hard power. For 10 points, name this kind of power.

Diplomat George Kennan's "Long Telegram" and X Article argued for this policy toward the Soviet Union, a strategy of preventing Communist expansion rather than rolling it back. For 10 points, name this Cold War policy adopted by the Truman administration.

This school of international relations, associated with Hans Morgenthau, holds that states act in their self-interest and seek power in an anarchic world. For 10 points, name this theory contrasting with liberalism.

This French aristocrat toured the young United States in the 1830s and wrote Democracy in America. He praised American civic associations but warned about the "tyranny of the majority." For 10 points, name this author.

This political philosopher wrote On Liberty, which defends individual freedom of speech and action unless it harms others. He also wrote Utilitarianism. For 10 points, name this English thinker, whose "harm principle" is named in the book.

In United States campaign finance, organizations of this type raise and spend money to elect or defeat candidates and are regulated by the Federal Election Commission. Super versions can raise unlimited sums but cannot coordinate with campaigns. For 10 points, name these groups, abbreviated PACs.

In this process held before general elections, voters or party members choose their party's nominee. A closed version limits participation to registered members of the party. For 10 points, name these elections, which include caucuses.

In this 1787 and 1788 series of eighty-five essays signed "Publius," Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay urged ratification of the Constitution. Number 10 warns about factions. For 10 points, name this series.

The writer of Federalist number 51 argued that "ambition must be made to counteract ambition," explaining this system in which each branch can limit the others. For 10 points, name this system, which includes the presidential veto.

In many countries, a government may hold this kind of direct vote in which citizens approve or reject a specific proposal, such as the 2016 United Kingdom vote on leaving the European Union. For 10 points, name this kind of direct vote.
This Greek philosopher's dialogue The Republic describes a just city ruled by philosopher-kings. His student Aristotle instead wrote Politics. For 10 points, name this teacher of Aristotle.
Answer these questions about political thinkers.
parts: Which Englishman wrote Leviathan?
Which Englishman wrote Two Treatises of Government?
Which Italian wrote Discourses on Livy as well as The Prince?

What kind of rule, adopted in 1917, allows debate to be ended with cloture?

parts: What term names a vote in which citizens decide a single policy question?

Which French political scientist formulated a "law" that plurality elections favor two parties?

q: Answer these questions about international relations.
parts: Which organization, headquartered in New York City, replaced the League of Nations?
Which 1648 settlement ending the Thirty Years' War is linked to state sovereignty?
Which American political scientist wrote The Clash of Civilizations?

q: Answer these questions about the Supreme Court.
parts: How many justices sit on the United States Supreme Court under current law?
What power, established in Marbury v. Madison, lets courts strike down laws as unconstitutional?
Who was the chief justice who wrote the Marbury opinion?

q: Answer these questions about forms of government.
parts: What term names rule by a single leader with absolute power?
What term names rule by a small number of people, such as a ruling clique?
What word, from Greek for "rule by the best," describes rule by a privileged elite?

q: Answer these questions about the Cold War.
parts: What wall, built in 1961, divided a German city?
Which policy, under Truman, pledged aid to nations resisting communism in Greece and Turkey?
Which 1947 American plan gave economic aid to Western Europe?

q: Answer these questions about the American system of government.
parts: Which document of 1787 is the supreme law of the United States?
Which amendment, ratified in 1791, includes freedom of speech, religion and the press?
Which 1819 case upheld the national bank and supremacy of federal law over states?

q: This amendment, ratified in 1791, protects freedom of speech, religion, the press, assembly and petition. It is the first of ten amendments added shortly after the Constitution was adopted. For 10 points, name this first part of the Bill of Rights.

The president can use this power to reject a bill passed by Congress. Congress can override it with a two-thirds vote in each house. For 10 points, name this presidential power, from the Latin for "I forbid."
